headline: Highest risk is medium: n8n can write and execute server-side workflows while oh-my-openagent injects MCP/hooks and broad network access, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and action-cascade paths.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: n8n can process workflow content and execute server-side nodes, while oh-my-openagent uses runtime-injected MCPs and hooks. That creates a plausible path for attacker-controlled content from one side to influence tool use on the other, even though no direct shared channel is documented. Uncertainty about the exact bridge keeps this below high.
conditions: IF n8n workflows ingest content originating from oh-my-openagent hooks or MCP outputs, prompt-like payloads can steer downstream tool calls.
IF either side treats file or message content as trusted instructions, injected directives can be executed.
mitigations: Disable automatic execution of untrusted workflow inputs.
Add provenance tags to all inter-agent messages.
Require human approval before tool calls triggered by external content.
Restrict MCP/hook inputs to allowlisted schemas.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation guards.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents have broad network egress and file access, and n8n explicitly handles server filesystem and per-credential secrets while oh-my-openagent touches project code, session history, and provider auth data. A shared workspace or connected system could leak sensitive data across the pair. The profiles do not prove a shared workspace by default, so medium is the safest supported level.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or connected system, files and secrets can cross from one agent to the other.
IF either agent uploads file contents to external services during normal operation, sensitive data can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Separate workspaces and credentials per agent.
Remove secrets from shared directories before running.
Disable unnecessary outbound integrations.
Review logs for file-content uploads.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage and network egress policy.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: n8n can write the server filesystem and execute commands, and oh-my-openagent runs with full-permissions mode plus broad network and subprocess capability. If both target the same mutable resources, concurrent writes or conflicting actions can corrupt state or overwrite each other. Because the profiles show overlapping write-like authority and no locking, high is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same directory or credential store, concurrent writes can race.
IF n8n Execute Command and oh-my-openagent full-permissions actions touch the same files, one can overwrite the other's state.
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories to each agent.
Avoid running both against the same git or config tree.
Serialize write operations with a lock file.
Turn off Execute Command for shared environments.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level resource locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: n8n is a workflow orchestrator that can act on outputs, and oh-my-openagent exposes task and message tooling plus browser and subprocess actions. If n8n consumes oh-my-openagent output as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into downstream actions without verification. The pair therefore has a direct action-amplification path.
conditions: IF n8n routes oh-my-openagent output into workflow actions without validation, incorrect facts can trigger side effects.
IF either agent is allowed to send messages or create tasks based on the other's output, errors can propagate downstream.
mitigations: Insert a verification step before any action-taking node.
Require structured outputs with schema validation.
Limit browser or subprocess actions to reviewed tasks.
Log and diff agent outputs before execution.
requires-engineering: add confidence gating for downstream automation.

E_compliance.rationale: n8n explicitly handles per-credential secrets and whatever the workflow processes, while oh-my-openagent touches project code, session history, and provider authentication data. That creates a plausible compliance mismatch around retention and sensitive-data handling, but the profiles do not show a specific residency or certification conflict. One-agent-only citations are insufficient here because the risk is pairwise data flow.
conditions: IF regulated data is processed through both agents, retention and logging policies must align.
IF one agent stores session history longer than the other, deletion/export obligations can diverge.
mitigations: Classify data before routing it to either agent.
Align retention settings across both systems.
Disable storage of sensitive prompts in session history.
Review vendor and deployment residency settings.
requires-engineering: implement unified deletion/export handling.
